derivations.claim: A real Banach space means a real normed linear space complete in its norm metric. This is the codomain condition in [F3] for the phrase “strongly measurable.” Write each $v\in H$ in its $d$ scalar coordinate classes $v^{(r)}\in L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R)$; the Definition gives the isometric finite direct-sum norm $\|v\|_H^2=\sum_{r=1}^d\|v^{(r)}\|_2^2$. If $(v_n)$ is Cauchy in this norm, meaning that for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ such that $\|v_n-v_q\|_H<\varepsilon$ for all $n,q\ge N$, then each coordinate sequence is Cauchy because $\|v_n^{(r)}-v_q^{(r)}\|_2\le\|v_n-v_q\|_H$. By [F8], each coordinate sequence converges to a class $v^{(r)}\in L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R)$. The finite tuple $v=(v^{(1)},\ldots,v^{(d)})$ belongs to $H$, and the finite sum of squared coordinate errors tends to zero, so $v_n\to v$ in $H$. Hence $H$ is complete and normed, so it is a real Banach space and [F3] applies.

Put $C_\phi=(\sum_{j=1}^m\|\phi_j\|_H^2)^{1/2}$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$, the triangle inequality and [F7] give
$$\|T(a)-T(b)\|_H\le\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\|\phi_j\|_H\le C_\phi|a-b|.$$
Thus $T$ is continuous and $U=T\circ A$ is Borel measurable. For each $n\ge1$, truncate every coordinate of $A$ to $[-n,n]$ and round it down to a multiple of $2^{-n}$, obtaining a finite-valued measurable map $A_n:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ with $A_n\to A$ pointwise. The maps $T\circ A_n$ are measurable simple $H$-valued functions and converge pointwise in norm to $U$ by continuity of $T$. Hence $U$ is strongly measurable by [F3].

For Borel sets $B\subseteq H$, the preimage map preserves complements and countable disjoint unions, and $U^{-1}(H)=\Omega$. Therefore $\mu(B)=\mathbb P(U^{-1}(B))$ is countably additive with $\mu(H)=1$ by [F2]. For any nonnegative Borel function $g:H\to[0,\infty]$, choose nonnegative simple functions $s_n\uparrow g$ as provided by [F5]. The identity $\int_H s_n\,d\mu=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[s_n(U)]$ follows by writing each simple integral as a finite sum over its level sets and using the definition of $\mu$. Apply [F6] to both sides and pass to the increasing limits to obtain $\int_H g\,d\mu=\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[g(U)]$. Apply this identity to the continuous function $g(v)=\|v\|_H^2$. The bound in step 1.2 with $b=0$ gives $\|U\|_H^2\le C_\phi^2|A|^2$, so $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\|U\|_H^2\le C_\phi^2\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}|A|^2<\infty$. This proves the stated moment identity and bound, and hence that $\mu$ is a finite-second-moment law of the Definition.

**General random-state interface.** Let $X$ be a specified separable real Banach space with its norm-Borel sigma-algebra, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, and let $U:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable: measurable finite-valued simple maps converge to $U$ in norm outside a measurable null set. A finite-second-moment state satisfies $\mathbb E\|U\|_X^2<\infty$. Finite collections of bounded linear maps $L_j:X\to\mathbb R$ are bounded sensors; their operator bounds are $|L_j(x)|\le C_j\|x\|_X$ with supplied finite $C_j$. When used as a physical model, specify whether randomness describes initial data, forcing, measurement, or an adopted stochastic closure. None of those interpretations follows from deterministic balance equations. This interface asserts no PDE or existence of a measurable solution selection.

**Spatial velocity law and integral sensor.** Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $(D,\mathcal D,\lambda)$ be a finite measure space with $0<\lambda(D)<\infty$, interpreted as a spatial region with volume measure $\lambda$. Let $H:=L^2(D,\lambda;\mathbb R^d)$ consist of almost-everywhere equivalence classes of measurable vector fields $v$ with $\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x)<\infty$, where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm. Give $H$ the norm $\|v\|_H:=(\int_D|v(x)|^2\,d\lambda(x))^{1/2}$ and its norm topology; this is the finite direct sum of the scalar $L^2$ norms. Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the norm-open subsets of $H$. A finite-second-moment random velocity law is a probability measure $\mu$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H))$ such that
$$\int_H \|v\|_H^2\,d\mu(v)<\infty.$$
For a sensor weight $\psi\in H$, define the ideal linear sensor and its centered observable by
$$S_\psi(v):=\int_D v(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,d\lambda(x),\qquad f_\psi(v):=S_\psi(v)-\int_H S_\psi(w)\,d\mu(w).$$
The sensor reads a weighted spatial average; it does not represent a point evaluation. When $v$ is assigned SI velocity units of metres per second and $\lambda$ is volume in $\mathrm m^d$, assigning $\psi$ units $\mathrm m^{-d}$ makes $S_\psi(v)$ a velocity. Other weight units multiply the sensor units by the corresponding factor. The centered observable is dimensionally the same as the sensor reading.

derivations.claim:
In the fixed Cartesian inertial chart of [F1], for each $k$ and coefficient vector $a$, the weighted sensor maps in [F2] and postulate [F5] use finite linearity of the pairings [F3] to give
$$(L_k(\Phi_k(a)))_i=S_{\psi_{k,i}}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_j\phi_{k,j}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}a_jS_{\psi_{k,i}}(\phi_{k,j})=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}[H_k]_{ij}a_j.$$
All terms are defined because $\phi_{k,j},\psi_{k,i}\in\mathcal H$ and [F3] makes each pairing finite. By the matrix definition in [F9], this is exactly the finite coefficient observation equation.
The finite coefficient equations, independent Gaussian vectors, PSD covariances, AC, and PD solved innovations satisfy the exact coefficient-filter proposition.

For each $k$, put $C_k=\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}\|\phi_{k,j}\|_{\mathcal H}$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^{m_k}$, the norm triangle inequality [F10] gives
$$\|\Phi_k(a)-\Phi_k(b)\|_{\mathcal H}\le\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}|a_j-b_j|\|\phi_{k,j}\|_{\mathcal H}\le C_k|a-b|,$$
because each coordinate satisfies $|a_j-b_j|\le|a-b|$. Thus $\Phi_k$ is continuous. This estimate is derived here; the finite-second-moment lemma [F4] does not assert continuity.

Apply [F7] to obtain the coefficient regular conditional kernel $\pi_k$ at every history. By step 1.2, $\Phi_k^{-1}(C)$ is Borel for every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. For each history $y$, $C\mapsto\pi_k(y,\Phi_k^{-1}(C))$ is a probability measure, and for each Borel $C$ its value is measurable in $y$ by the kernel property; hence $\rho_k$ is a probability kernel. For any Borel observation-history set $B$, the defining conditional-law identity in [F8] therefore gives
$$\mathbb P(U_k\in C,\ y_{1:k}\in B)=\mathbb P(a_k\in\Phi_k^{-1}(C),\ y_{1:k}\in B)=\int_B\pi_k(y,\Phi_k^{-1}(C))\,\nu_k(dy).$$
The last integrand is $\rho_k(y,C)$, so the conditional event identity holds for $U_k$ and $\rho_k$ is its regular conditional law by [F8]. Because $\pi_k$ is defined at every history, so is its pushforward $\rho_k$, including on null histories.

Since $|e|=1$, $\|\phi\|_{L^2}^2=\int_D|e|^2\,d^3x=V<\infty$ and $\|\psi\|_{L^2}^2=\int_D|e/V|^2\,d^3x=1/V<\infty$. Linearity of the sensor integral gives
$$S_\psi(\phi)=\int_D e\cdot(e/V)\,d^3x=V/V=1,$$
so the scalar observation matrix is $H_1=1$.

The chosen state transition and process noise give forecast mean $m_{1|0}=\mu$ and variance $P_{1|0}=P$. Thus the innovation covariance is $S_1=H_1P_{1|0}H_1^T+R=P+R>0$, the gain is $K_1=P/(P+R)$, and the covariance update is
$$P_{1|1}=P-\frac{P^2}{P+R}=\frac{PR}{P+R}.$$
Substituting $v_1=y_1-\mu$ into the mean update gives the displayed $m_{1|1}$. These formulas hold at $P=0$ as well because $R>0$.
